children.text: An open-air heritage resort where dozens of Spanish- and American-era mansions, dismantled and moved from across the Philippines or faithfully reconstructed, stand between a river and the sea. Guided tours, raft rides, and horse-drawn carriages let you walk through a 19th-century Philippine street.

Las Casas Filipinas de Acuzar is a heritage resort at the mouth of the Umagol River in the village of Bagac, on the western coast of the Bataan Peninsula. Real estate developer and antique-house collector Jose "Jerry" Acuzar bought Spanish colonial- and American-era mansions from across the Philippines that were at risk of collapse, dismantled them piece by piece, numbered the timber and bricks, and had them moved here and rebuilt. Since opening around
, dozens of mansions have lined the riverbank, forming a single old-time village.
Acuzar began rebuilding old mansions in Bagac in

, and today more than 60 relocated or reconstructed mansions and over 30 structures such as bridges, arches, plazas, fountains, and canals stretch along the river mouth on a site of about 400 hectares. Tulay ni Lola Basyang, the bridge across the Umagol River, is modeled on an old bridge over Manila's Pasig River, and there is also a small church, the Sanctuario de San Jose, as well as a torogan, a royal house of the Maranao people of Mindanao. In
the resort joined Historic Hotels Worldwide, and in
the association named it "Best Historic Hotel in Asia/Pacific."

The village is lined with rows of bahay na bato, the traditional Philippine mansion style with a stone ground floor and a wooden second story, and the cobblestone plazas, arched bridges, church-like buildings, and canals combine to create the feeling of standing in the middle of a 19th-century street in Binondo or Vigan. Notable examples include Hotel de Oriente, a recreation of the old Binondo hotel where Jose Rizal once stayed; Casa Hidalgo, whose façade was moved from a mansion in Quiapo, Manila; and Casa Byzantina, known for its Byzantine-style ornamentation.

The village is also frequently used as a filming location for Philippine period dramas, movies, and weddings. At the same time, it has drawn steady criticism for removing cultural heritage from its original localities, making it a place that also invites reflection on the tension between preservation and commercialization.

It suits travelers who love architecture, history, and photography, and expats who want to show visiting family from abroad a different side of the Philippines. Behind the resort is a beach facing the South China Sea (West Philippine Sea), so you can combine cultural exploration with beach relaxation in one trip.
The heart of the day tour: a guide explains each mansion's original location and owners, its architectural style, and how it was moved here. The tour takes around
1 hour
, and you can go inside some of the mansions. You take off your shoes every time you enter a mansion, so slip-on shoes are the most convenient.
This recreation of the Philippines' first luxury hotel, which opened in Binondo, Manila, in
, is the symbol of the resort. The hotel is known as the place where Jose Rizal stayed in Room 22 in
, and its lobby and staircase full of wood carvings, along with its façade reflected in the water, are popular photo spots.
Ride a bamboo raft slowly along the canals and river, viewing the riverside mansions from the water. It's especially beautiful at sunset.
Ride a horse-drawn carriage, once a means of transport in old Manila, along the cobblestone streets. It isn't included in the day tour, so you pay about
per person separately, and one ride loops around for about
12–15 minutes
Rent a Maria Clara dress or a barong tagalog, traditional Filipino attire, and take photos in front of the mansions. It's especially popular for family photos.
The resort's beach is a quiet stretch of gray sand facing west, making for beautiful sunsets.
If you're staying overnight, take a walk through the village after dark, when the streetlamps and windows light up. A completely different, old-world atmosphere unfolds from daytime.
Casa Hidalgo, built in Quiapo, Manila, in
, was the home of painter Rafael Enriquez; the University of the Philippines School of Fine Arts held classes there until
, training painters such as Fernando Amorsolo. Casa Byzantina, built in San Nicolas, Manila, in
, is the building where the University of Manila first opened in
, and Casa Unisan, built in Unisan, Quezon Province, in
, now houses a restaurant serving Filipino home cooking.

From Manila, take NLEX up and switch to SCTEX, then head down the Bataan Peninsula along the Roman Superhighway from Dinalupihan. Near Balanga, cross the peninsula via the Pilar–Bagac road to arrive. It's about
160km
and takes
3–4 hours
, with toll costs of about
one way. From Clark, it takes about
2 hours
Instead of entering central Balanga, stay on the Roman Superhighway and turn right under the Alauli intersection flyover in Pilar onto Governor J.J. Linao National Road. After about
20–25 minutes

on a winding two-lane mountain road over the foothills of Mount Samat, you'll reach the Philippine-Japanese Friendship Tower, a white concrete tower at the entrance to Bagac town; turn left here and follow the coastal road to the resort's main gate. This Bagac–Pilar road is also the route walked by the prisoners who set out from Bagac on the Bataan Death March on
April 11, 1942
. Tolls on NLEX and SCTEX are paid with an Easytrip RFID, so top up your balance generously, and to avoid the traffic leaving Manila, get through NLEX before
6 AM
Take a Balanga-bound bus (Bataan Transit, Genesis, etc.) from Cubao, Avenida, Pasay, and so on. It takes about
3–4 hours
and costs about
. From the Balanga terminal, take a jeepney or minibus bound for Bagac or Morong for about
45 minutes–1 hour
(about
) and get off at the Philippine-Japanese Friendship Tower, Bagac's white obelisk, then go about
10 minutes
by tricycle (about
). By public transport it takes nearly
5 hours
each way, so a day trip is tight and one night's stay is recommended.

Jeepneys bound for Bagac often wait a long time until they fill up, so it is quicker to take one bound for Morong, which passes the same Friendship Tower and leaves more often. If the destination on a bus's windshield is Mariveles, first ask the conductor whether it enters the Balanga terminal. Tell the tricycle driver to drop you at Gate 5, where day-tour guests and overnight guests check in.
Genesis buses leave from its terminals at EDSA Cubao and Pasay Rotonda (below MRT-3 Taft Avenue Station) about every
30 minutes
from around
4 AM

, and Bataan Transit buses also run from Cubao to Balanga. If you have a lot of luggage or are traveling in a group, you can also hire a whole tricycle (a "special" trip) in Balanga to go straight to the resort; agree on the fare before you get in.
If you're flying in from abroad, Clark International Airport (CRK) is the closest. From the airport, it's about
2 hours
by rental car or chartered van. From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), it takes
3–4 hours
The 1Bataan ferry used to run in about
1 hour
from the Esplanade Seaside Terminal in Pasay, Manila (behind SM Mall of Asia) and the terminal near the CCP to Capinpin port in Orion, Bataan (
when bought on site), with a free shuttle from the port to Balanga, but as of
service is suspended indefinitely. Check the latest announcements on whether it has resumed, and even if it is running, you still need about
40 minutes–1 hour
more by vehicle from Balanga to Bagac.
Travel agency day tours from Manila usually leave at
3–4 AM
and return at
8–9 PM
, include a round-trip private van, tolls, and day-tour admission, and often stop at Mount Samat Shrine on the way back. Prices depend on group size, at about
per person: cheapest with around 12 people and most expensive with 2. Check whether lunch is included and whether the admission is based on the weekday or weekend rate.
Bataan's west coast has a clear-cut dry and wet season. The
November–May
dry season is best, and
December–February
in particular is pleasant for outdoor walking tours thanks to a cool sea breeze.
March–May
has very strong midday sun, so it's best to do the tour in the morning.
During the
June–October
wet season, the southwest monsoon (Habagat) hits directly, bringing frequent rain and rough seas. Tours still run in the rain, but raft and beach activities may be limited. In
July–September
, some days see roads closed due to typhoon effects.
Around
April 9

, Araw ng Kagitingan (Bataan Day / Day of Valor), a commemorative event is held at the Mount Samat war memorial, and lodging fills up early over the year-end holidays and Holy Week. If photography is a priority,
November
, right after the wet season when the sky is clear and the greenery is lush, is recommended.
The
Holy Week holidays (Maundy Thursday to Easter Sunday) fall on
March 25–28
, and
April 9
, the Day of Valor, is a Friday, making a three-day weekend, so book early for these dates. On the other hand, weekday lodging discounts come up often in the wet season, and the
monsoon sale offered up to 50% off, so if you keep an eye on the weather and go on a weekday, you can save a lot on accommodation.

Accommodation inside the resort is distinctive for being relocated old mansions converted into guest rooms. Spending a night in a room with hardwood floors, capiz-shell windows, and antique furniture is an experience that's part of the trip itself. Rates run high, about
a night, though larger family-sized rooms are available. To save on budget, it's better to stay at a budget-to-midrange beach resort in Bagac or nearby Morong (about
a night) and visit on a day tour.
There are also hotel-style rooms (for 2–6 people) that cost less than the old mansion rooms, at about
a night based on the official website listing. Check-in is at
3 PM
and check-out at
12 noon
, and at check-in you leave a refundable deposit of

in cash. Inside the resort are Kusina ni Nanay Maria for Filipino home cooking, La Bella Teodora for Italian, Cafe del Rio for Spanish tapas, and the beachside Dapitan Bar, all operating first come, first served without reservations.

Overnight guests start the day with a buffet breakfast at Binondo Hall. Kusina ni Nanay Maria, on the first floor of Casa Unisan, serves Filipino home cooking such as pinakbet (vegetable stew), kilawin tanigue (Spanish mackerel cured in vinegar), and saging con yelo (banana with shaved ice), while Cafe del Rio serves Spanish tapas and ham and cheese platters. If you get hungry while strolling, try the Filipino street food and kakanin (rice cakes) at La Parilla & Pica-Pica. Well-known Bataan specialties include tinapa (smoked milkfish), bagoong (shrimp paste) and patis (fish sauce) from Mariveles, and bibingka (rice cake) from Abucay and Balanga, all good buys at the Balanga market.

Day tours also accept walk-ins, but booking on the official website must be made by the day before your visit, and full payment must be made within two days after booking. Accommodation and activities fill up early on weekends and holidays, so book in advance.
Guided tours depart at set times. Check the departure time when booking and arrive at least
30 minutes
beforehand.
The walking tour is mostly on outdoor cobblestone paths. Bring comfortable sneakers, a hat, a parasol, and water.
The best light for photos is
8–9 AM
or after
4 PM
. At midday the sunlight is so strong that white walls get blown out.
Drone photography and commercial shoots require prior permission. Wedding and pre-wedding photo shoots also carry an extra fee.
Bagac town has few ATMs, and they often run out of cash. Withdraw enough cash in Balanga beforehand.
If traveling by public transport, the last Balanga–Bagac service ends early, so set off before
4 PM

Among the private casas, Casa Gapan, Casa Balanga, and Casa Irosin share the semi-private pool of "Island II." One dog or cat may be brought along only when staying in a private casa; vaccination records, a deposit, and a cleaning fee are required, and pets are not allowed in hotel rooms or indoor common areas.
The day tour rate is
on weekdays and

on weekends and some public holidays, and includes a welcome drink, a guided walking tour, a visit to Hotel de Oriente, the raft, lunch (a meal credit on some weekdays), and beach access. Children aged 4 and under are free, ages 5–10 are half price, and day-tour guests can stay from
8 AM to 6 PM
. Check the latest rates on the
official website
You must show ID at entry, and an environmental fee under a Bagac ordinance (
per person, valid throughout Bagac for 4 days) is charged separately. Outside food is not allowed; if you bring any, you must pay a corkage fee of
per food item.
The Bagac environmental fee (

per person) is collected only by uniformed municipal or barangay staff with ID, who give you an official receipt and a ticket with a serial number. Don't pay anyone on the road who separately demands an entrance fee or environmental fee, and keep your ticket safe, since you'll need to show it at Bagac's other beaches and attractions for 4 days.
Most of the furniture and decorations inside the mansions are genuine antiques. Don't touch or lean on them, and follow the posted occupancy limits on stairs and balconies.
The midday walking tour feels very hot. Watch for heatstroke in elderly visitors and children, and have them rest in the shade often.
During the wet season and monsoon periods, the beach can have high waves and rip currents. Avoid swimming when no lifeguard is on duty.
There are a lot of mosquitoes around the river and canals in the evening. Be sure to bring insect repellent.
The mountain roads on the Bataan Peninsula are winding with few streetlights. Avoid driving at night if possible.

If you book and don't show up, the full booking amount is charged as a no-show fee. If you booked through a travel booking site, changes and cancellations follow that site's policy, so check the change conditions first during the typhoon-prone wet season.
